subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 24-year-old man is found to have total cholesterol of 296 mg/dL and LDL cholesterol of 210 mg/dL during an employment screening; he is asymptomatic. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 41, and his paternal grandmother had a similar lipid pattern. LDL cholesterol is also elevated in his 12-year-old daughter.
question: Which of the following patterns of inheritance best explains this family's lipid abnormality?
explanation_correct: Familial hypercholesterolemia is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so heterozygous relatives in successive generations have elevated LDL; heterozygotes occur in about 1 in 500 people. Transmission through the paternal line to a daughter excludes X-linked inheritance, and the trait appears in every generation. Homozygotes are very rare but far more severely affected.

explanation_incorrect.A: An autosomal recessive pattern would require both parents to be carriers and would not produce this vertical, multi-generation pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: An affected father cannot pass an X-linked recessive disease to a daughter as an affected phenotype; she would be a carrier.
explanation_incorrect.D: X-linked dominant inheritance from an affected father affects all daughters but no sons, which does not fit this pedigree.
explanation_incorrect.E: Mitochondrial inheritance is strictly maternal, but this trait came through the paternal side.

educationalObjective: Familial hypercholesterolemia is an autosomal dominant disorder with vertical transmission and a heterozygote frequency of about 1 in 500.
